summary:
The page completes the **TensorFlow** `train_step` begun on p.250. After computing the loss with `self.compute_loss`, it takes `tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)` and calls `self.optimizer.apply(gradients, self.trainable_weights)` exactly as in Listing 7.21. Then comes the new part: a loop **`for metric in self.metrics:`**. If `metric.name == "loss"` the metric is updated with the loss value (`metric.update_state(loss)`); otherwise it is updated with `metric.update_state(targets, predictions)` (callout: updates the model's metrics, including the one that tracks the loss). The step returns **`{m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}`**, a dict mapping metric names to their current value (callout).

To try it, `get_custom_model()` is redefined so that `compile()` now receives **`optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam()`, `loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()` and `metrics=[keras.metrics.SparseCategoricalAccuracy()]`**; the architecture (784 inputs, Dense 512 relu, Dropout 0.5, Dense 10 softmax) is unchanged, and training is again `model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)`. The progress bar should now show both `loss` and the accuracy metric.

Under *train_step() metrics handling with PyTorch*, the authors note that it is **exactly the same code change**. The PyTorch `CustomModel` computes predictions with `self(inputs, training=True)`, the loss with `self.compute_loss(y=targets, y_pred=predictions)`, calls `loss.backward()` and gathers `gradients = [v.value.grad for v in trainable_weights]`. The page breaks here; the weight update under `torch.no_grad()`, the metric loop and the return are on p.252, followed by the JAX version, which uses `compute_loss()` inside `compute_loss_and_updates()`.

code.title: get_custom_model() compiled with loss and metrics, and training
code.original_code:
def get_custom_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = CustomModel(inputs, outputs)
    model.compile(
        optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(),
        loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(),
        metrics=[keras.metrics.SparseCategoricalAccuracy()],
    )
    return model

model = get_custom_model()
model.fit(train_images, train_labels, epochs=3)
code.what_it_does: Redefines the model factory so that compile() supplies loss and metrics for self.compute_loss and self.metrics, then trains.

code.title: PyTorch train_step with compiled loss and metrics (first part; continues on p.252)
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def train_step(self, data):
        inputs, targets = data
        predictions = self(inputs, training=True)
        loss = self.compute_loss(y=targets, y_pred=predictions)

        loss.backward()
        trainable_weights = [v for v in self.trainable_weights]
        gradients = [v.value.grad for v in trainable_weights]

deeper.title: Why dispatch on metric.name?
deeper.body: Keras metrics share the method name `update_state`, but not its arguments. A `Mean`-style loss tracker takes one value; `SparseCategoricalAccuracy` takes `(y_true, y_pred)`. `self.metrics` mixes both kinds, so the loop needs to tell them apart. The book's code uses the loss tracker's name, `"loss"`. Beyond the book: Keras 3 also offers `self.compute_metrics(x, y, y_pred)`, which does the update and return in one call. The book does not mention it on this page.

deeper.title: Reading the progress bar
deeper.body: Beyond the book: with this version, each epoch line shows something like `loss: 0.29 - sparse_categorical_accuracy: 0.91`. Both are running averages over the epoch so far, reset automatically at each epoch because they are in `self.metrics`. A callback such as `EarlyStopping(monitor="sparse_categorical_accuracy")` can now monitor accuracy, which wasn't possible with Listing 7.21's loss-only logs.

questions.question: In the metric loop, why does the code check metric.name == "loss"?
options: Because the loss tracker is updated with the loss value, while other metrics take targets and predictions
Because only the loss metric needs resetting
Because metric names must be unique
questions.answer: Because the loss tracker is updated with the loss value, while other metrics take targets and predictions
questions.explanation: The two branches call update_state with different arguments. The loss metric isn't skipped; resetting is handled by fit(); uniqueness is unrelated.

questions.question: What does the train_step return, and what does it contain for the model compiled on this page?
questions.answer: {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}, containing the loss and the sparse categorical accuracy.
questions.explanation: self.metrics includes the compiled SparseCategoricalAccuracy plus the loss tracker (p.250).

questions.question: Compared to p.248, what changed in get_custom_model() and why?
questions.answer: compile() now also receives loss=SparseCategoricalCrossentropy() and metrics=[SparseCategoricalAccuracy()], because the new train_step uses self.compute_loss and self.metrics instead of global objects.

questions.question: Which line differs between the PyTorch train_step on p.248 and the one starting on this page (up to the gradient collection)?
questions.explanation: p.248 used loss_fn(targets, predictions); the other lines are identical.

questions.question: Why is the training accuracy reported by this train_step likely lower than the accuracy from evaluate() on the same data?
questions.answer: Because predictions are computed with training=True, so Dropout(0.5) is active, and because the reported value averages over an epoch during which the model was still improving.
questions.explanation: Inference from the code: metrics are updated with training-mode predictions.
